name: Pongamia oil

lead: Pongamia oil (karanja oil) is pressed from the seeds of Pongamia pinnata, also called Millettia pinnata or Indian beech. In Ayurvedic and Unani traditions it has been applied to the skin for itching, abscesses and other skin complaints, and it is used in soapmaking and rural cosmetics. People interested in skin appearance encounter it as a traditional skin oil and as an ingredient in some redness-targeted formulas.

The seeds hold roughly 27-40 percent oil, about half oleic acid, plus flavonoids such as karanjin and pongamol. A 2018 laboratory and clinical-cosmetic study evaluated pongamia oil alongside three other compounds for effects on inflammatory and vascular responses linked to rosacea; most published work on the oil, however, concerns biofuel and agriculture.

paras: Traditionally the oil is applied topically, often mixed with other herbal preparations, and it appears in soaps. In modern cosmetics it is an ingredient in some formulas rather than a stand-alone product.

The oil's flavonoids give it a bitter taste and odour, and ingesting it can cause nausea and vomiting. Seed-cake feeding studies in animals report toxicity effects at high replacement levels. Anyone with sensitive skin may react to a botanical oil; product labels advise patch testing.

chain: Oil applied topically or in soap
angle.text: Traditional users apply the oil to irritated or blemished skin, and a formulation containing it has been studied for rosacea-related redness. The appearance benefit is mostly described in traditional use.

lead: Pongamia oil, also known as karanja oil, is a non-edible vegetable oil pressed from the seeds of the tree Pongamia pinnata (Millettia pinnata), native to parts of Asia and Australia.[1][2] The seeds contain about 27-39 percent oil, nearly half of it oleic acid.[2]

For appearance, the oil's main role is as a traditional skin preparation. Ayurvedic and Unani practice has applied it to the skin for itches, abscesses and ulcers, and it is used in soapmaking and rural cosmetics.[3][1] Its bitter flavonoids, including karanjin and pongamol, are credited by proponents with antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity.[2][3]

Published research is mostly about biofuel, lubricants and pest control. A 2018 study in Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dermatology evaluated pongamia oil together with dextran sulfate, 4-t-butylcyclohexanol and hesperidin methyl chalcone for effects on inflammatory and vascular responses implicated in rosacea, a facial redness condition.[4]

paras: The tree is a fast-growing leguminous evergreen, also called karanja or Indian beech, and is native to the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia and northern Australia.[2][3] Its oil has served as lamp oil, a lubricant and a soap ingredient, and is among the best-studied non-edible oils for biodiesel.[2][1]

Traditional Ayurvedic and Unani practice uses the oil topically for itching, abscesses, ulcers and other skin conditions, often combined with other herbs.[3] It is also used in soap production and rural cosmetics.[3][1] A review of the tree's applications notes medicinal, insect-repellent and soap uses.[1]

No stand-alone human trials of pongamia oil for appearance were found. A 2018 study assessed pongamia oil as one of four compounds, with dextran sulfate, 4-t-butylcyclohexanol and hesperidin methyl chalcone, on inflammatory and vascular responses implicated in rosacea.[4]

The oil's flavonoid compounds can cause nausea and vomiting if ingested.[2] In a trial in ram lambs, replacing soybean meal with 75 percent detoxified karanja cake reduced body weight and some reproductive measures, showing that the seed by-products have biological effects in animals.[5]
